label: Damascus Document (Brit Damesek) — Part 2 — Columns 9–16
summary_plain: The second half of the Damascus Document contains the Laws section — detailed legal rulings governing community life. Rules for judges: ten judges shall be elected, four from the tribe of Levi and Aharon and six from Yisra’el. Rules about oaths, witnesses, and restitution. Shabbat laws are strict: do not carry, do not kindle fire, do not walk beyond the prescribed distance. Rules for the assembly of the camps: families arranged by tribes. Rules for the overseer (mevaqqer) who instructs the community. The document concludes with warnings about the final visitation and the coming of the Mashiach of Aharon and Yisra’el.
summary_scholarly: Columns 9-16 of the Damascus Document constitute the Laws section (Serekh), providing the most detailed halakhic code from Qumran outside the Temple Scroll. The laws govern a community organized in ‘camps’ (makhanot) — not a single monastic settlement but a network of scattered communities. The Shabbat code is stricter than later rabbinic halakhah in several respects. The judicial system requires tribal representation (Levi and Yisra’el). The overseer (mevaqqer) functions as an instructor and pastoral leader. The reference to the ‘Mashiach of Aharon and Yisra’el’ indicates a dual-messianic expectation: one priestly, one royal. The Qumran legal material preserves a pre-rabbinic legal tradition independent of the Mishnah and Talmud.

key_terms.definition: The Damascus Document Part 2 requirement: no accusation may stand on the testimony of a single witness. Two or three witnesses must agree. This protects community members from arbitrary punishment — a stricter evidentiary standard than the Jerusalem Temple's practice.

The Damascus Document's detailed regulations on oaths in cols 9-16: oaths may not be taken in the full Name of YHWH in a binding way outside the covenant entry process. Oaths are taken by the covenant of the Torah only.

The Damascus Document Part 2 contains extensive Sabbath rulings stricter than mainstream practice: no tool may be used, no trade conducted, no travel beyond a measured distance, no assistance to animals. Among the most detailed Sabbath regulations in the DSS corpus.

Overseer — the community official responsible for admitting new members and overseeing the camp. Instructs members in the works of the Torah and adjudicates disputes. Must be between 30 and 60 years old, master of languages and community rule.

The process by which new members join the covenant community in the Damascus Document: examined by the Paqid, instructed in all the rules, and admitted after probation. Entry is voluntary but subject to strict examination.

The list of offenses and punishments in cols 9-16: community members who lie about property, bear false witness, murmur against the community, or violate specific laws face suspension or expulsion. Graduated penalties based on offense severity.
Property of the Many — communal funds managed by the Paqid. Members contribute a minimum of two days' wages per month to the common fund for the poor and needy of the community.

The Damascus Document specifies that each camp must have a panel of judges — four from Yisra'el and three from Levi and Aharon — a total of ten, echoing the biblical requirement for a quorum of judges.

Separation — the Damascus Document's core principle: maintaining separation between the pure and impure, the covenant community and outsiders, the Sabbath and the work week. Separation is covenant discipline, not social isolation.

The camp arrangement — the Damascus Document describes communities living in camps in towns and villages, governed by the Damascus covenant rules. This distinguishes the broader movement (camp members) from the desert Qumran Yahad community.

faq.question: What is the main content of Damascus Document Part 2?
faq.answer: Columns 9-16 form the legal section (the Serekh or Order) of the Damascus Document. Part 2 contains the community's penal code, Sabbath laws, oath regulations, witness requirements, the role of the Paqid (Overseer), rules for admitting new members, and management of communal property. These are the operational rules for covenant communities living in towns and villages across the land — the Damascus communities rather than the isolated Qumran Yahad.

faq.question: How strict are the Damascus Document's Sabbath laws?
faq.answer: Among the strictest in any ancient Jewish text. Members may not carry anything from house to house or in the field, may not engage in trade, may not travel beyond a measured distance, may not assist animals in difficulties, may not prepare food, and may not use any tool. The Sabbath begins when the sun is a specified distance from the horizon on the sixth day. These rules are more restrictive than the Jerusalem Temple's practice, reflecting the community's belief that the Temple establishment had allowed the Sabbath to be corrupted.

faq.question: What does the two-witness rule mean for the community?
faq.answer: It is a protection against arbitrary accusation. No matter may be established on the word of one person. Two or three witnesses must independently agree. If a member witnesses a violation and cannot find a second witness, they must confront the offender directly first. Only after that confrontation fails, and a second witness is established, can the matter be brought before the judges. This applies within the community — it is about internal covenant accountability.

faq.question: What is the role of the Paqid (Overseer)?
faq.answer: The Paqid is the camp administrator: they admit new members, instruct members in the works of the Torah, adjudicate disputes, manage the communal fund, and oversee camp life. The Paqid must be between 30 and 60 years old, master of every secret of men and every tongue, gentle and resolute. Each camp has one Paqid. The position is not the same as the high priest or the Teacher of Righteousness — it is a practical administrative and pastoral role.

faq.question: What is the communal fund and who benefits?
faq.answer: Members contribute at least two days' wages per month to the hand of the Paqid and judges. This fund supports the poor, the needy, the elderly, those struck by plague, those taken captive, the unmarried, those without family. It is a structured mutual-aid system embedded in the covenant community's legal framework. The Damascus Document's fund is distinct from the more total property-pooling of 1QS (Community Rule).

faq.question: How does one enter the Damascus covenant community?
faq.answer: Entry is examined by the Paqid: the candidate is questioned about their knowledge of the Torah and willingness to follow the community's rules. After instruction in all the rules, the candidate takes an oath binding themselves to the covenant of the Torah of Moshe. Entry is voluntary but once entered, the person is bound by the full penal code. Violation of the rules leads to suspension or, for serious offenses, expulsion.

faq.question: What offenses lead to expulsion?
faq.answer: Among the most serious: bearing false witness against another community member, deliberate violation of the Sabbath after being warned, speaking the full Name of YHWH in blasphemy, murmuring against the Many, betraying the community to outsiders, and violating sexual regulations. Lesser offenses result in graduated suspensions. The gradation between suspension and expulsion reflects the distinction between intentional and unintentional violation.

faq.question: How do the Damascus Document's camps differ from the Qumran Yahad?
faq.answer: The camps were ordinary towns and villages — the Damascus Document governed a broader movement of covenant-keeping people who lived in society, married, had families, and held property (while contributing to a common fund). The Qumran Yahad (1QS) was a more intensive community that pooled all property fully and separated more completely from society. Both operated under covenant law but the camps were the more accessible form of the movement.

faq.question: What is the significance of the oath laws?
faq.answer: They restrict when and how the Name of YHWH may be invoked. Oaths are sworn by the covenant of the Torah only — not casually, not as a rhetorical device, not by the full divine Name. This is consistent with the broader DSS reverence for YHWH's Name. The oath laws also prevent manipulation of the community's legal process through false religious invocations.

faq.question: How does the Damascus Document Part 2 differ from Part 1?
faq.answer: Part 1 (cols 1-8) is the Admonition — a theological and historical narrative describing the community's origins, the Teacher of Righteousness, the Man of the Lie, the Three Nets of Belial, and the community's covenant identity. Part 2 (cols 9-16) is the Serekh — the practical legal code that governs daily life. Part 1 explains why the community exists; Part 2 explains how the community operates day to day. Together they form a complete community charter.
